turns.zh: 我知道导入错误数据会给你的客户带来各种痛苦、迅速失去他们的信任。Christina，谢谢你来，如果想了解更多，去 OneSchema.co，就是 OneSchema.co。好，回到 AI 和它對 SEO 的影响，你能用 AI 帮上这个忙吗，能用 AI 为你创造内容吗？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: AI is a tool. Everyone says AI is a tool, it's not a solution. You can use AI to create content if the content you're creating is a part of that journey. For example, before AI content really came on the scene, because AI's been around for a while, Jasper's been around for a while, Writer's been around for a while before ChatGPT. Before these tools, a lot of ways that companies created content for cheap is they went on Fiverr, and they went on Upwork, and they just created content. (01:00:20): A lot of that content, completely worthless. If you're just creating content for the sake of content, and you paid someone on Upwork $50 for their content, now you can use an AI tool and just create the content, the same worthless content, for free. AI as a tool is a tool creating something that's not necessarily useful for the end journey of the company and for the user journey in general. However, if the content you were creating was pretty useful, and now you're using AI to create really useful content for cheaper and better, of course, you can use it. (01:00:53): An example of a place you can use AI content is if you're an e-commerce site and you're selling your own products, of course, you can use AI content to write product descriptions. It's not a content website. There's a lot of big companies out there, and if anybody wants to look at some of the e-commerce sites and how they do SEO, a lot of them have large SEO teams. The typical JCPenney, the Nordstroms, the Macy's, they have a lot of content on their category pages, but if you look at the keywords that drive traffic to those pages, it's the products on the pages. (01:01:25): If you're looking for shoes, the fact that a Macys.com page will have a lot of content about what shoes do doesn't do anything for the user. They're just looking for shoes, and then there's shoes on the page. I think Macy's actually ranks pretty well on those kinds of things. Using AI content to write more fluff content that's not necessary would just be a waste of time. (01:01:46): Using AI content to feed in a product, and describe what that product is, and maybe some features of that product which help a user, that's not hurting your SEO, because what you're trying to optimize for is the product and the product name itself.
turns.zh: AI 是个工具。每个人都说 AI 是工具，它不是方案。如果你在造的内容是那个旅程的一部分，你可以用 AI 造内容。比如，在 AI 内容真正登场之前——因为 AI 已经存在一阵子了，Jasper 存在一阵子了，Writer 在 ChatGPT 之前就存在一阵子了——在这些工具之前，很多公司廉价造内容的方式是上 Fiverr、上 Upwork，就造内容。那些内容很多完全一文不值。如果你只是为了内容而造内容，你在 Upwork 上花 50 刀让人写的内容，现在你可以用 AI 工具免费造出同样一文不值的内容。AI 作为工具，是个在造不一定对公司最终旅程、对整体用户旅程有用之物的工具。然而，如果你造的内容本来就有用，而现在你用 AI 更便宜、更好地造出真有用的内容，那当然可以用。能用 AI 内容的一个地方是，如果你是个电商网站、在卖自己的产品，当然你可以用 AI 内容写产品描述。它不是个内容网站。外面有很多大公司，如果有人想看一些电商网站怎么做 SEO，很多都有庞大的 SEO 团队。典型的 JCPenney、Nordstrom、Macy's，他们的分类页上有很多内容，但如果你看驱动那些页面流量的关键词，是页面上的产品。如果你找鞋子，一个 Macys.com 的页面有很多关于“鞋子是啥”的内容，对用户毫无用处。他们就找鞋子，然后页面上有鞋子。我觉得 Macy's 其实在那类东西上排得相当好。用 AI 内容写更多不必要的废话内容，纯属浪费时间。用 AI 内容去喂一个产品、描述那产品是什么、也许还有帮用户的某些产品特性，那不会伤害你的 SEO，因为你优化的是产品和产品名本身。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Basically, don't use AI to generate entire blog posts. I know people are doing this all over the place, but absolutely leverage AI to help you add to existing pages, descriptions, titles, things like that, which I can see why Google, Google would've no idea that you were helped to write this thing with AI, right, if it's just a small part of the page versus the entire page?
turns.zh: 明白了。基本上，别用 AI 生成整篇博客。我知道人们到处这么干，但绝对可以用 AI 帮你加到现有页面、描述、标题这类东西上，而我能理解为什么 Google 根本无从知道这东西是 AI 帮写的——对吧，如果它只是页面的一小部分、而不是整个页面？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: In their documentation, they say that AI itself is not the problem. It's the helpfulness, the usefulness of the content that would be a problem.
turns.zh: 在他们的文档里，他们说 AI 本身不是问题。成问题的是内容的有用性、实用性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You don't have to name names or reveal anything, but do you know of a bunch of companies using AI now to generate tons of high successful pages, high converting pages in some way? In this way?
turns.zh: 你不必点名或透露什么，但你知道现在有一批公司用 AI 生成大量高成功、高转化的页面吗？用这种方式？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: There's this hatred of AI content by users in general. I think once companies declare that they're using AI, people get upset about it. It was a Red Ventures company, I think it was CNET that said they were using AI to create content. I think they got in trouble because they said they're using AI to create content, but if they had not said they're using AI to create content, I think their entire model would've been very successful. (01:03:09): There's no reason you can't take in, they take 10 products, and they want to review 10 different products. There's no reason you can't tie that all together, have AI write the original piece of content, and then have a human editor just review it. I don't know, years ago, it's not AI, but it's sort of like AI, but there are sports websites that will take in a lot of the things that happen in the sports game to merge it all together into a piece of content. (01:03:34): If you look at any earnings reports on public companies, it's sort of the same thing. Their company will issue, they'll file their earnings report, and then now it's AI. Before AI, it was basically like Mad Libs kind of content. It would extract pieces of the earnings report and then it would write a blog post, which is actually fairly useful. I don't think there's an issue with it itself. I don't think users have an issue with it. (01:03:56): I think if you read that old piece of content, again, on earnings reports, it's pretty obvious that it wasn't written by a financial journalist, but it was useful. You got a quick summary, you didn't have to go into the SEC and read an earnings report.
turns.zh: 用户对 AI 内容整体上是有敌意的。我觉得一旦公司宣布他们用 AI，人们就 upset。有个 Red Ventures 的公司，我想是 CNET 说他们在用 AI 造内容。我觉得他们惹了麻烦是因为他们说自己用 AI 造内容，但如果他们没说，我觉得他们整个模式会非常成功。没理由你不能拿进来——他们拿 10 个产品，想评测 10 个不同产品。没理由你不能把它们全串起来，让 AI 写初稿，然后让人类编辑审一下。我不知道，几年前，那不是 AI，但有点像 AI，有些体育网站会把体育比赛里发生的很多事串成一篇内容。如果你看任何上市公司的财报，有点像同一回事。他们的公司会发布、会提交财报，然后现在用 AI。在 AI 之前，基本上是像 Mad Libs 那种内容。它会抽取财报的片段，然后写一篇博客，其实相当有用。我觉得它本身没问题。我觉得用户对它没意见。如果你读那篇旧内容，再次，关于财报，很明显不是财经记者写的，但它有用。你拿到个快速总结，不必去 SEC 读财报。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's this guy, Noah Smith, he's on Twitter, he's got a newsletter called No Opinions. It's awesome. He had this tweet about how we're approaching an age of a ton of slop of content, just a lot of really bad content generated by AI for better or worse, this is related to SEO, but it makes me think about just how much bad stuff we're going to see. (01:04:28): To your point, it doesn't matter whether it was generated by AI or not, people will gravitate towards and Google will gravitate towards stuff that is useful and good, whether it's written by people or not.
turns.zh: 有个家伙 Noah Smith，在 Twitter 上，他有个 newsletter 叫 No Opinions。很赞。他有条推文讲我们正 approaching 一个大量垃圾内容、就是大量 AI 生成的真的烂内容的时代，不管好坏，这跟 SEO 相关，但让我想到我们会看到多少烂东西。按你说的，不管它是不是 AI 生成的，人们会 gravitate 向、Google 也会 gravitate 向有用和好的东西，不管是不是人写的。

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: This is a huge issue for Google, because the amount of content being created is enormous, and it's growing exponentially. Google's trying to crawl everything. They now have more content to crawl, which becomes more expensive for Google, and which is why you have this backlash by Google against many websites, because they're trying to clean the index to save their own costs and to protect the users from having to see this awful content.
turns.zh: 这对 Google 是个大问题，因为被创造的内容量巨大，而且在指数级增长。Google 试图爬一切。他们现在有更多内容要爬，对 Google 来说更贵了，而那就是为什么你有 Google 对很多网站的反弹，因为他们在试图清理索引、省自己的成本、保护用户不必看到这些糟糕内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The crazy thing for LLMs is now to be trained. They're trained on content on the internet in a big way, and they're struggling with not training their LLMs on stuff that AI has written because it becomes this, a bad direction that LLMs will go. They're trained on themselves. Anyway, something I wanted to come back to around AI, which is AI Overviews. I imagine many people are like, "How do I get into that answer? How do I get my product into the answer that Google gives at the top?" Is that something you recommend people try to do? Is that something you can do?
turns.zh: 对 LLM 来说疯狂的是现在要训练。它们在很大程度上用网上的内容训练，而它们在挣扎于不拿 AI 写的东西训练自己的 LLM，因为那会变成 LLM 会走的糟糕方向。它们是被自己训练的。总之，我想回到关于 AI 的一点，就是 AI Overviews。我想象很多人在想“我怎么进那个答案？我怎么让我的产品进到 Google 顶部给的答案里？”这是你建议人们试着做的吗？这是你能做的吗？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: I think of AI or AI Overviews as a branding exercise. Getting into the AI Overview, and Google has links, I mentioned this earlier that Google has links within the content, and I think a lot of what Google does is around potentially liability protection. They're having links. They're saying, "Well, we didn't tell you to jump off the Golden Gate Bridge, this website, which we summarized, told you to jump off the Golden Gate Bridge," or, "We didn't plagiarize. We just linked to the piece of content. We may have extracted more from the content than we were supposed to, and the law hasn't decided that yet, but we linked to it, so it's fair." (01:06:17): Right now, Google has these links in the content, and it sort of links off of it. I did a survey on LinkedIn, and I was surprised by the answer. I thought most people did not click on the links. I got a couple hundred responses, and it's sort of 50/50 and based on my SurveyMonkey experience. It's not a statistically significant survey in general, but it will never go to 99% and one. That's fairly indicative that people are clicking the links, which surprises me, because I don't think that the links are necessarily meant by Google to be useful, which means that AI Overviews is essentially duplicating search results. (01:06:53): You have this AI Overview which summarizes, then you have a link so you can link off of it, and then beneath it, you sort of have the exact same thing. That's the challenge that Google has to work through. For a company to show up in AI Overview, it's a brand challenge. If your link shows up there, then you likely were showing up beneath it in the ranking results, so you've already done the work you're supposed to do. (01:07:12): If you're showing up in the AI Overview mentioned as a brand, like, these are the top CRM tools, you're showing up as a brand, that means you've exercised brand efforts and it's working out. I don't know that companies necessarily want their content to show up because they're giving away their content for free. They want to be showing up in a way that benefits them. If you show up as a brand, you've done good branding, but if you show up as a link, it means Google has stolen your content, and people may or may not click off of it.
turns.zh: 我把 AI 或 AI Overviews 当成品牌动作。进到 AI Overview，而 Google 有链接——我早先提过 Google 在内容里有链接，而我觉得 Google 做的很多是围绕潜在的责任保护。他们有链接。他们说“嗯，我们没叫你从金门大桥跳下去，是这个网站——我们总结的那个——叫你跳的”，或者“我们没抄袭。我们只是链到那篇内容。我们可能从内容里抽取的比该抽的多，法律还没定，但我们链了，所以公平。”现在 Google 在内容里有这些链接，它某种程度上从那链出去。我在 LinkedIn 做了个调查，答案让我惊讶。我以为大多数人不会点那些链接。我拿到几百个回复，大概是 50/50，而且基于我的 SurveyMonkey 经验，总体上它不是统计显著的，但它永远不会到 99% 对一个。那相当说明人们在点那些链接，这让我惊讶，因为我不觉得 Google 放那些链接本意是有用的，这意味着 AI Overviews 本质上在复制搜索结果。你有个 AI Overview 做总结，然后你有个链接能从那链出去，然后在它下面，你基本有完全一样的东西。那是 Google 得想透的挑战。对一家公司要出现在 AI Overview 里，这是个品牌挑战。如果你的链接出现在那，那你很可能本来就在下面的排名结果里出现了，所以你其实已经做了你该做的。如果你作为品牌出现在 AI Overview 里被提到，比如“这些是最好的 CRM 工具”，你作为品牌出现，那意味着你做了品牌努力、而且奏效了。我不知道公司是否一定想让自己的内容出现，因为他们在免费送出自己的内容。他们想以对自己有益的方式出现。如果你作为品牌出现，你做了好品牌；但如果你作为链接出现，那意味着 Google 偷了你的内容，人们可能会或可能不会从那点出去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along this lines of brand and SEO, do you have any... That's always this question of are we investing in brand? Do we just want people to be aware we exist, or are we trying to actually drive conversion? Any advice on how to think about brand building and SEO, especially with this world of AI?
turns.zh: 顺着品牌和 SEO 这条线，你有没有……一直有这个问题：我们是在投品牌吗？我们只是想让人知道我们存在，还是我们真在试图驱动转化？关于怎么思考品牌建设和 SEO，尤其在这个 AI 世界里，有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: The biggest myth in SEO is that you could just build links, and link building is the secret source and the secret sauce to growing your SEO footprint. That's totally wrong, because the way most people build links is they buy these guest posts, or they pay for links on low authority websites that sort of look like they might have authority, and it doesn't really benefit anyone because no one's reading these sites. (01:08:22): It's funny that everyone complained about Google as this really, really smart, all-knowing LLM, and at the same time, they think they're dumb enough to fall for these guest posts that are on websites that no one really read. The right way to build links is to build a brand. It comes part and parcel of what you're trying to do. If you're building links, and going back to all the SaaS examples we talked about, so if you've created a bunch of content that is not relevant for the product you're trying to sell, building links to the content that doesn't really benefit the product, doesn't really benefit, the links don't benefit the product. (01:08:55): If you can build this product that's awesome and everyone loves and wants to use, and you get not links, but mentions, and links might be mentions now, because the way a link before LLMs and the link 10 years ago was actually an HTML link. Now, Google can read content. They can say, "Well, you've been mentioned here," that's pretty good. Now, we acknowledge that this might be the brand, and this might be the match for that kind of thing. (01:09:23): That's helping to build that brand. In general, I think of any SEO effort as promoting a brand, building up a brand, rather than building a product, and then separately building out an SEO effort, which has content that may not be relevant, and links from websites that are certainly not relevant to content that's not relevant. It all comes together as being one big effort. The same thing you'll do on PR, you'll do for SEO.
turns.zh: SEO 里最大的迷思是你能就建外链，而建外链是增长你 SEO 版图的秘密来源和秘密配方。那完全错了，因为大多数人建外链的方式是买这些客座文章，或是在低权威、看起来可能有点权威的网站上付费买链接，而它其实不造福任何人，因为没人在读这些网站。好笑的是，每个人都抱怨 Google 是个真的、真的聪明、全知的 LLM，同时却又觉得它蠢到会中这些在没人读的网站上的客座文章的招。建外链的正确方式是建品牌。它跟你试图做的事是一体的。如果你在建外链，回到我们聊的所有 SaaS 例子，如果你造了一堆跟你想卖的产品不相关的内容，给不真正造福产品的内容建外链，那些外链不造福产品。如果你能造出这个超棒、人人爱用想用的产品，你拿到的不是外链，而是提及——现在外链可能就是提及，因为 LLM 之前、十年前链接的方式是个真正的 HTML 链接。现在 Google 能读内容。他们能说“嗯，你在这被提到了”，那就相当好。现在，我们承认这可能是那个品牌，这可能就是那种匹配。那在帮着建那个品牌。总体而言，我把任何 SEO 动作都当成在推广品牌、建起品牌，而不是建一个产品、然后另外再搞个 SEO 动作——有跟产品可能不相关的内容、从不相关的网站来的外链。它全部合起来是一个大动作。你在 PR 上做的，也是为 SEO 做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. I'm glad we touched that. There's a few other directions I want to go, so I'm going to bounce around a little bit and cover some of the other stuff I wanted to extract from your deep experience in this space. One is you've mentioned this idea of programmatic SEO a couple times versus editorial. Maybe first, just clarify what those two directions are, just for people that don't exactly know what you mean. Then two, what's your general advice for which direction to go, programmatic or editorial?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好。很高兴我们聊到这个。还有几个别的方向我想去，所以我会稍微跳着聊、覆盖一些我想从你这个领域深经验里挖出来的别的东西。一个是你提过几次的程序化 SEO vs 编辑式这个想法。也许先就为不太确定你意思的人澄清这两种方向是什么。然后二是，对走哪个方向——程序化还是编辑式——你一般的建议是什么？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: It might be obvious at this point, but I'm going to say it's dependent on the user, but essentially, what programmatic is is it's taking a bunch of data sources and building out a page that is a combination of all these data sources. In my book, I talk about two of my favorite programmatic SEO companies. One of them was created by a past, well, it's not created, the strategy was created by a past guest of yours, Luc Levesque, who introduced us, and that was TripAdvisor. (01:10:50): TripAdvisor took in all these data sources of, "This is the hotel, these are the cities," and then it allowed UGC to combine into one comprehensive page about each property. TripAdvisor did not write a piece of content on every single hotel. They don't write a piece of content on, "Here's this long form blog post as an influencer on the Waldoff Astoria of New York, and here's a long form blog post about the Marriott Marquis in San Francisco." (01:11:17): They built it all from a programmatic standpoint. They took all these data sets, they took all the countries in the world, they took all the properties, and they merged into one comprehensive page, which has dominated the top of search results since the beginning of the time. They still own it. That team has cycled through many, many leaders, many different, a lot of different things, and they're still number ones. It's the strategy that has allowed them to build that brand and to dominate it. (01:11:43): The second example is Zillow. What Zillow did is they solved an early problem many years ago in the real estate space, which is no one understood what the value of a piece of property was. Zillow took in all of those data sets. They got, some of them are government data sets, some of them are their own comparison data sets based on other home sales. The government can say a house is worth one price, and based on their comparison, Zillow can completely disagree with it. (01:12:11): They're building in these data sets, and they're taking photos from realtors, they're taking neighborhood data, they're taking school data, and that's a programmatic SEO page. SEO is the only channel to bring in traffic to each one of these pages. They're not going to do paid traffic for my house, they're not going to do paid traffic for your house. The only way someone would find that page on Zillow, either they start at Zillow.com and then just navigate through it, or they Google it. Those are programmatic SEO efforts. (01:12:38): On the flip side is editorial. Editorial would be, in TripAdvisor's case, writing out that long form piece of content around each hotel, each city, and all the things they've done. Zillow would be the same. Zillow would take 500 million properties and write out an editorial piece of content. Neither of those would be a fit for their model, and it would be extremely expensive. Say each piece of content would cost a thousand dollars, that would be cost prohibitive for anyone to do. (01:13:06): Going back to my distinction based on the user, what is it that the user's looking for? Is the user looking for the value of a home? They don't need a long form piece of content. They need a piece of content or a page that just says what the value of that home is. TripAdvisor's case, they're looking for a single thing, a rating, or maybe they need some of that UGC, but really, they're looking for that rating. That long form piece of content, there's a purpose for it, but not on TripAdvisor's site. (01:13:31): Understanding, what is it that the user needs will help solve, do you approach this from an editorial standpoint, or do you approach this from a programmatic standpoint? Some of the companies I mentioned earlier, like G2 and Capterra, which are completely being disrupted, so they're being disrupted by editorial, but they're also being disrupted by Google itself with their AI Overviews. (01:13:53): If you look for the top CRM tools, you have G2 or you have Capterra, but you also have Forbes writing out a long form piece of content on what Salesforce is, what HubSpot is, and that's probably unnecessary.
turns.zh: 到这会儿可能 obvious 了，但我说它取决于用户，不过本质上，程序化是拿一堆数据源、建出一个综合了所有这些数据源的页面。在我的书里，我聊了我最喜欢的两个程序化 SEO 公司。其中一个是由你的一个前嘉宾、把我们介绍给彼此的 Luc Levesque 创造的策略——是 TripAdvisor。TripAdvisor 拿进所有这些数据源——“这是酒店，这些是城市”——然后它让 UGC 结合进每个物业的一篇综合页面。TripAdvisor 没为每一个酒店写一篇内容。他们不会写“这是一篇长内容博客，作为影响者写纽约的 Waldoff Astoria，这是一篇长内容博客写旧金山的 Marriott Marquis”。他们从程序化角度全建了。他们拿所有这些数据集、拿世界上所有国家、拿所有物业，合并成一篇综合页面，从一开始就在搜索结果顶部称霸。他们现在还占着。那个团队换过很多很多领导、很多不同的事，他们还是第一。那是让他们建起那个品牌、称霸它的策略。第二个例子是 Zillow。Zillow 做的是多年前解决了房地产领域一个早期问题：没人理解一处房产的价值是多少。Zillow 拿进所有那些数据集。他们拿到一些政府数据集，一些基于别的房屋销售、他们自己的比较数据集。政府能说一栋房子值某个价，而基于他们的比较，Zillow 完全可以不同意。他们在建这些数据集，拿房产经纪人的照片、拿社区数据、拿学校数据，而那是个程序化 SEO 页面。SEO 是把流量带进这些页面的唯一渠道。他们不会为我的房子做付费流量，不会为你的房子做付费流量。有人找到那个 Zillow 页面的唯一方式，要么从 Zillow.com 开始然后导航过去，要么 Google 它。那些是程序化 SEO 动作。另一面是编辑式。编辑式在 TripAdvisor 的情况，是给每个酒店、每个城市写那篇长内容，以及他们做的所有事。Zillow 也一样。Zillow 会拿 5 亿处房产、写一篇编辑式内容。那两个都不适合他们的模式，而且会极其贵。假设每篇内容花 1000 刀，对任何人来说都成本高到 prohibitive。回到我基于用户的区分，用户在找什么？用户在找一处房子的价值？他们不需要一篇长内容。他们需要一个页面、就说那房子价值多少。TripAdvisor 的情况，他们在找一个单一的东西、一个评分，或也许需要点 UGC，但真的，他们在找那个评分。那篇长内容有用处，但不在 TripAdvisor 的站上。理解用户需要什么，会帮着解决你该从编辑式角度、还是程序化角度切入？我早先提的一些公司，像 G2 和 Capterra，正被彻底颠覆——所以他们在被编辑式颠覆，但也在被 Google 自己的 AI Overviews 颠覆。如果你找顶级 CRM 工具，你有 G2 或 Capterra，但你也有 Forbes 写的长内容讲什么是 Salesforce、什么是 HubSpot，而那大概没必要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think generally, you would, programmatic is the better path and the most common success path is what I'm hearing. What are things you need in place to be successful in programmatic SEO? Like basically, you just need some sort of data source that you own. Is that just... What's a checklist of like, "Here's what tells you you have a big opportunity here?"
turns.zh: 我觉得一般来说，你会说程序化是更好的路、最常见的成功之路，这是我听到的。要在程序化 SEO 上成功，你需要就位什么？基本上，你只需要某种你拥有的数据源。就只是……有什么样的清单，比如“这告诉你在这里有大机会”？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: Programmatic is the right solution when there's scale and when there's a user use case. If there is not, you create scale for nothing. An earlier version of programmatic, again, pre a lot of the internet companies now, is building out a piece of content for every single zip code in America. Say you offer some sort of local product. You would build out a page for every single zip code that is, in theory, programmatic, but users don't look for it, and Google has completely disrupted that with their own local products. (01:15:02): Programmatic can always be something. I see programmatic mistakes all the time, where websites look at, they say, "Look, we're making reviews of software. There's 10,000 different softwares in the world. We're just going to make out a page for each one and we're going to combine it with, I don't know, a city." You can make programmatic pages like that, but there's no use case. Really knowing what programmatic solution to use comes down to, "Is this something that someone would actually be looking for? Does this page itself provide a solution?" Zapier provided a solution because someone was looking for that combination, but there are many tools like Zapier, which try to be Zapier, but they're not looking for that solution. Going back to some of the template companies you mentioned, I don't think a lot of companies that make templates, they're making programmatic, but there's not a use case for every single one of those templates. They've made programmatic for no [inaudible 01:15:53]. (01:15:54): Again, SurveyMonkey was one where we had a fat head of templates we could make, but it wasn't a long tail. We could make a hundred templates, but we couldn't make 10,000.
turns.zh: 当有规模、当用户有用例时，程序化是正确的方案。如果没有，你造规模造了个寂寞。程序化的一个更早版本——再次，在很多现在的互联网公司之前——是给美国每一个 zip code 写一篇内容。假设你提供某种本地产品。你会给每一个 zip code 建一个页面，理论上那是程序化，但用户不找它，而 Google 已经用自己的本地产品彻底颠覆了那个。程序化永远能是某种东西。我一直看到程序化错误，网站看——他们说“看，我们在做软件评测。世界上有 1 万个不同软件。我们就要给每一个建个页面，再跟，我不知道，一个城市结合。”你能造那样的程序化页面，但没有用例。真的知道用哪个程序化方案，归结于“这是有人真的会找的东西吗？这个页面本身提供一个方案吗？”Zapier 提供了方案，因为有人在找那个组合，但有很多像 Zapier 的工具，想成为 Zapier，但他们不在找那个方案。回到你提的一些模板公司，我不觉得很多做模板的公司——他们在做程序化，但那些模板不是每一个都有用例。他们为了没有[听不清]而做了程序化。再次，SurveyMonkey 是个我们有一大把能做的模板、但不是长尾的例子。我们能做一百个模板，但做不了 1 万个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to do a rapid fire of SEO myths. Before I do that, I know that you spent a lot of time actually reading the recent ruling against Google and their whole deal with Apple, and you were telling me it revealed there were a lot of interesting stuff about their strategy and where search was going. Let's spend a little time here, just what did you learn doing that exercise?
turns.zh: 我想来一波 SEO 迷思快问快答。在那之前，我知道你花了很多时间真的读了最近对 Google 的裁决、以及他们跟 Apple 的整个交易，你跟我说它揭示了很多关于他们策略和搜索走向的有趣东西。我们在这花点时间，你做那个练习学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: It's fascinating. It's 286 pages. I basically read a book. It was a verdict.
turns.zh: 太迷人了。286 页。我基本是读了一本书。那是个判决书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, geez.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: I would say that the judge or the clerk that wrote this verdict has a better understanding how the SEO works and how digital marketing works than most people I meet in digital marketing.
turns.zh: 我会说，写这个判决书的法官或书记官，比我在数字营销里遇到的大多数人，更懂 SEO 怎么运作、数字营销怎么运作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I did not expect to hear that.
turns.zh: 哇，我没料到会听到这个。

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: Yeah. This verdict explains how Google decides to rank a page. The verdict explains how the auction model works in ads, in Google Ads. I think that's fascinating. Talked about the comparison between social media. This court really understood a lot of the questions that were posed to them. For example, Google tried to say that they're not a monopoly because they're social media. The court analyzed that question and said, "Social media is not a comparison to Google search." (01:17:12): Google tried to say a lot of the things they did were non-monopolistic because there's alternatives like Bing. The court really analyzed a lot of these things. Why I found it fascinating was, again, a lot of the testimony was public, is the summary of how the court put it all together in a verdict. A few of the things I learned is one, the market share, Google's market share. That's been a number that no one really liked to talk about. (01:17:39): Google would say, "Oh, we think it's like 80%," because they didn't want to be viewed as a monopoly. Microsoft would say, "Well, maybe we have 20%." I just found a recent document from Microsoft where they claimed to have a lot of market share in search. In the verdict, it says that Google has 98% of mobile searches. I forget whether it said that the court said it, and it said Google didn't disagree, or that came from Google's own documentation, but 98% of mobile searches. (01:18:08): The thing that I thought was most fascinating from the verdict is how much the default partnerships that Google has contributes to Google's success. The plaintiff in the case was the Department of Justice suing Google for being a monopoly. However, I don't know what the word is, but one of the complainants in this is this company, Neva, which was a search engine started by a past Google, I think it was like a head of research or something. A senior person at Google created a new search engine. (01:18:39): A lot of the trial was focused on how Neva could not be successful, despite having a better search engine, despite having a better experience for users, because they didn't have any of these default distribution agreements. That's the part that I thought was most fascinating. Google has these default agreements with Apple, and they also have Chrome. (01:18:58): They have all these inputs into Google searches, which means that I don't think there's a chance, and this is the biggest takeaway, I don't think there's a chance that ChatGPT, or Perplexity, or Claude, or any of these other LLM startups, because they're startups now, even OpenAI is a startup with Microsoft's investments, still a startup. I don't think they have a chance at really unseating Google purely from a quality standpoint. (01:19:27): That's what a lot of the documentation in this verdict is about is how much a force of habit, how much the brand, and how much the distribution agreements Google has, drives searchers to Google. There were a couple of very interesting insights. One is that Bing tried to give itself to Apple for free, and Apple said there was absolutely no price that they would take to use Bing search within Apple. (01:19:49): Another one was Mozilla had a partnership with, I think it was Yahoo, and they did a rev share deal with Yahoo, and everyone switched back to Google. When people say, "Well, SEO is dead, everyone's going to go to OpenAI," and you just look at the 25 years of Google's existence and what they've built, I really don't think so. I really think distribution and the force of brand will keep almost everything Google has today. (01:20:14): Now, why is Google fighting back so hard to build AI Overviews? Well, I think there's two answers. One is, like I said, Wall Street. They really want Wall Street to think that they care and they're doing this thing. The other is losing small percentage points to ChatGPT costs Google a lot of money, so it's worth it for them to invest in it, but I don't think that they have any fear about not being the most dominant search engine in the world.
turns.zh: 对。这个判决书解释了 Google 怎么决定一个页面的排名。判决书解释了广告拍卖模型在 Google Ads 里怎么运作。我觉得那很迷人。聊了跟社交媒体的比较。这个法院真的理解了很多抛给他们的问题。比如，Google 试图说他们不是垄断，因为他们是社交媒体。法院分析了那个问题，说“社交媒体不是跟 Google 搜索的可比对象”。Google 试图说他们做的很多事不是垄断的，因为像 Bing 这样的替代存在。法院真的分析了很多这些事。我觉得它迷人的原因是，再次，很多证词是公开的，是法院怎么在判决书里把一切串起来的总结。我学到的几件事之一是，市场份额，Google 的市场份额。那是没人真喜欢谈的数字。Google 会说“哦，我们觉得大概 80%”，因为他们不想被视为垄断。Microsoft 会说“嗯，也许我们有 20%”。我刚找到一个 Microsoft 最近的文档，他们声称在搜索上有很大市场份额。判决书里说 Google 有 98% 的移动搜索。我忘了它说的是法院说的、Google 没反对，还是那来自 Google 自己的文档，但移动搜索的 98%。我觉得判决书里最迷人的是，Google 那些默认合作伙伴对 Google 成功的贡献有多大。这个案子的原告是司法部告 Google 垄断。然而，我不知道那个词怎么翻，这个案子里的申诉者之一是 Neva，一个由前 Google 人——我想是研究主管之类的——创立的搜索引擎。Google 的一个资深人士创了个新搜索引擎。很多庭审聚焦在 Neva 怎么可能不成功——尽管有更好的搜索引擎、尽管有更好的用户体验——因为他们没有任何那些默认分发协议。那是我觉得最迷人的部分。Google 跟 Apple 有这些默认协议，而且他们还有 Chrome。他们有所有这些进入 Google 搜索的入口，这意味着我不觉得有机会——这是最大的 takeaway——我不觉得 ChatGPT、Perplexity、Claude、或任何这些别的 LLM 创业公司有机会，因为他们现在是创业公司，连 OpenAI 有 Microsoft 投资也是个创业公司，还是创业公司。我不觉得他们有机会纯粹从质量角度真正扳倒 Google。判决书里很多文档讲的就是习惯的力量、品牌的力量、Google 拥有的分发协议，有多大程度把搜索者引向 Google。有几个非常有趣的洞见。一个是 Bing 试图把自己免费给 Apple，而 Apple 说绝对没有任何价格他们会接受在 Apple 内用 Bing 搜索。另一个是 Mozilla 跟——我想是 Yahoo——有过合作，他们做了个跟 Yahoo 的收入分成交易，然后所有人都切回了 Google。当有人说“嗯，SEO 死了，大家都要去 OpenAI”，你只要看 Google 存在的 25 年、以及他们建的东西，我真不觉得。我真觉得分发和品牌的力量会保住 Google 今天几乎拥有的一切。现在，为什么 Google 这么努力反击、去建 AI Overviews？嗯，我觉得有两个答案。一个是，像我说的，华尔街。他们真的想让华尔街觉得他们在意、在做这个事。另一个是，丢掉给 ChatGPT 的小几个百分点，对 Google 来说花很多钱，所以对他们来说投资它是值得的，但我不觉得他们对“不会是世界上最主导的搜索引擎”有任何恐惧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, isn't the idea with this trial that this may change, and they may lose that default status, whether it happens or not, that's the whole game here, right? It's like maybe they can't be that anymore, and that maybe opens up. I think that's the opportunity potentially.
turns.zh: 嗯，这个审判的点不就是这个可能会变、他们可能失去那个默认地位——不管发生不发生，这才是整个游戏，对吧？就像也许他们不能再那样了，而这也许打开了局面。我觉得那才是潜在的机会。

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: I don't think so. Yeah, I'm no legal expert. I don't know what the DOJ will do, but what's interesting, if you saw Google's press release when the verdict came out, so Google tweeted, "We thank the court for recognizing that we're the greatest search engine in the world, and more to come." They're going to fight back, and it's almost like a bully being declared the world's greatest bully. They're like, "See, told you we're strong." (01:21:15): When reading the verdict, it actually said, "There is no competitor. Google is the greatest search engine. They have 25 years of great data. They've done a fantastic job." I don't see any way that those, if they break the default agreements, Apple actually loses all that money Google's paying, and then users will still Google. That's not what will do it. I think the only thing they can do is figure out how to prop up a competitor.
turns.zh: 我不这么认为。对，我不是法律专家。我不知道 DOJ 会做什么，但有趣的是，如果你看判决书出来时 Google 的新闻稿，Google 发了推文：“我们感谢法院承认我们是世界上最伟大的搜索引擎，而且还有更多。”他们会反击，就像个被宣布为世界最强恶霸的恶霸。他们就像“看，早说我们强了”。读判决书时，它其实说“没有竞争者。Google 是最伟大的搜索引擎。他们有 25 年的好数据。他们做得极棒。”我不觉得如果他们打破那些默认协议，Apple 其实会丢掉 Google 付的所有那些钱，然后用户还是会 Google。那不是会做到的事。我觉得他们唯一能做的，是想出怎么扶起一个竞争者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I think that's an interesting takeaway. People will go to Google, will switch to Google even if it's not default. There's actually a really interesting takeaway from Ben Thompson's analysis of this stuff, and I will point to the podcast episode. I think that shifted my perspective on this, because when you hear Google is paying Apple to be the default search engine, it sounds nefarious and unfair. The deal is actually revenue share. They give them a percentage of the revenue from the ads, which ends up being $20 billion, something like that, a lot of money for Apple. Anyone else can come to Apple and say, "We will give you a revenue share of our searches also." It's just nobody is as big and can pay as much. If you think about it, why can't Google come to Apple? "Hey, we will send you tons of money by doing the search for you and giving you a large percentage of the ads that we are doing for you." (01:22:36): It's weird to not allow that if you really think about it, but it's also unfair, because no one else will ever be able to compete with that.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得那是个有意思的 takeaway。人们会去 Google，就算不是默认也会切到 Google。其实 Ben Thompson 对此的分析有个真有意思的 takeaway，我会指一下那期播客。我觉得那转移了我对这个的视角，因为当你听到 Google 付 Apple 钱当默认搜索引擎，听起来很邪恶、不公平。那个交易其实是收入分成。他们给 Apple 广告收入的一个百分比，最后变成 200 亿刀，对 Apple 是笔大钱。任何别人也能去 Apple 说“我们也给你搜索的收入分成”。只是没别人那么大、能付那么多。你想想，Google 为什么不能去 Apple 说“嘿，我们为你做搜索、把我们做的广告里很大一个百分比给你，会送你一大笔钱”？如果你真想想，不允许那个很怪，但它也不公平，因为没别人永远能跟那个竞争。

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: Yeah, and that's what the court said is like Neva didn't have a chance because of that. One other point is, so I did this survey, this was years ago when I was at SurveyMonkey, I did a search market penetration survey to figure out who used what, like Bing versus Google. On my survey, I was generous. I threw DuckDuckGo on there, and I came back, I had thousands of responses, and came back that I had 1% of people use DuckDuckGo. (01:23:07): I didn't realize it, that DuckDuckGo didn't actually know what their market penetration was. When I shared the survey, Gabriel Weinberg, who's the CEO of DuckDuckGo, hit me on Twitter and he said, "Can you share the data with us? We really would like to see it." This was, let's say 10, 12 years ago. In the verdict, it said that DuckDuckGo's market share is 2%. I came back with 1% 12 years ago. DuckDuckGo, I think they raised a hundred million dollars. (01:23:33): They have all these brand partnerships. They have, at baseball games, they have their logo, they've done everything, and all they've been able to do is get from 1% to 2%. There's a lot there, and Google being Google, I don't see anyone knocking them off.
turns.zh: 对，那也是法院说的——Neva 因为那个没机会。另一点是，我做过这个调查，是几年前我在 SurveyMonkey 时，我做了个搜索市场渗透率调查，弄清谁用什么，Bing vs Google。在我的调查里我很 generous。我加了 DuckDuckGo，回来时我有几千个回复，回来显示 1% 的人用 DuckDuckGo。我当时没意识到，DuckDuckGo 其实不知道他们自己的市场渗透率是多少。当我分享调查时，DuckDuckGo 的 CEO Gabriel Weinberg 在 Twitter 上找我，说“你能把数据分享给我们吗？我们真的很想看。”那是，假设 10、12 年前。判决书里说 DuckDuckGo 的市场份额是 2%。我 12 年前回来是 1%。DuckDuckGo，我想他们融了 1 亿刀。他们有所有这些品牌合作。他们在棒球赛上有 logo，他们做了一切，而他们唯一能做到的，是从 1% 到 2%。那里有很多东西，而 Google 是 Google，我不看到任何人能扳倒他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating. Well, thanks for sharing your takeaway so that we don't have to read this report. Before I move to rapid fire SEO myths, is there anything else along the lines of AI or SEO that you think is really important to share that you want to leave listeners with?
turns.zh: 迷人。好，谢谢你分享你的 takeaway，这样我们就不必读这份报告了。在我进入 SEO 迷思快问快答之前，还有没有什么关于 AI 或 SEO、你觉得特别重要、想留给听众的？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: I think the most important thing to leave people with is SEO is not dying. There will always be a world where users are requesting their own information. One of the reasons I think these home assistants, whether it's from Google, or Apple, or Amazon, have never taken off, is because you don't have choice. You talk to your Google, and it gives you only one answer. You talk to Amazon, and it gives you only one answer. Like, "I want to buy toilet paper," and Amazon just buys you whatever it decides to buy you. (01:24:33): There will always be a world where there needs choice. One other piece from the verdict is Google believes that we're in the very early days of LLMs, and even with all the machine learning they do and understanding users, you will always need real user data, which Google has on past searches. I think users will always be requesting their own information, and there's never going to be an AI that understands you so perfectly, it's going to know that for you personally, you would like to click result number five. (01:25:01): That's the best fit for what you're looking for right now, which means that there always needs to be multiple choices to make. Yes, most clicks are probably going through the first one, two, or three results, but there needs to be seven, 10, multiple pages of Google, because some people do go to those other pages. I think that's the most important thing to underscore is that all of this means that search changes, a lot of top-of-funnel search goes away, but in general, there's always going to be a world where people are doing the searches. (01:25:33): Then the last piece on that really is when you're looking to do something with search, you're looking to take an action. Companies benefit from those actions. Say you're a hotel, and you want people to sleep in your hotel and pay you to sleep in your hotel. The aggregate number of people needing to take that action and pay you for it does not change even if search volume gets cut. If you're selling shoes, people still need to buy shoes. (01:25:58): If you're selling information, though, your media, if you're WebMD, yes, your revenue declines, because that information that you now aggregated and curated and gave away for free in return for people clicking on ads, Google is now going to give away for free in return for no one clicking on ads.
turns.zh: 我觉得留给人们最重要的事是 SEO 没在死。总会有一个世界，用户自己在索取自己的信息。我觉得这些家庭助手——不管是 Google、Apple 还是 Amazon 的——从没起飞的一个原因是，你没有选择。你跟你 Google 说，它只给你一个答案。你跟 Amazon 说，它只给你一个答案。像“我想买厕纸”，Amazon 就给你买它决定给你买的。总会有一个世界需要选择。判决书里的另一点是，Google 相信我们处在 LLM 很早的阶段，即使有他们做的所有机器学习、对用户的理解，你永远需要真实的用户数据，而 Google 在过往搜索上有。我觉得用户永远会自己索取信息，也永远不会有个 AI 完美理解你到这种程度——它为你个人知道你会想点第五个结果，那是你现在找的东西的最佳匹配，这意味着永远需要多个选择去做。对，大多数点击大概通过第一、二、三个结果，但需要七、十个、多页的 Google，因为有些人确实去那些别的页面。我觉得最要强调的就是，所有这一切意味着搜索在变、很多顶层漏斗搜索消失，但总体而言，总会有一个世界人们在做搜索。然后那上面的最后一点真的是，当你想用搜索做点事，你想采取个行动。公司从那些行动受益。假设你是个酒店，你想让人睡你的酒店、付钱睡你的酒店。需要做那个行动、付钱给你的人数总量，即使搜索量被砍，也不会变。如果你在卖鞋，人们还是需要买鞋。但如果你在卖信息，你的媒体，如果你是 WebMD，对，你的收入下降，因为你现在聚合、策展、免费给出、换人们点广告的信息，Google 现在会免费给出、换没人点广告。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. I wonder if there's an investment arbitrage opportunity of predicting which businesses will decline with this and which will thrive. Anyway, I want to talk about SEO myths. I know that you have a few things, and we've talked about a few of these, I think, of just things that you know people believe about SEO, but they're actually wrong. Let me just ask you, what are some myths that people get wrong about SEO?
turns.zh: 有意思。我想知道有没有个投资套利机会，去预测哪些生意会随这个衰退、哪些会繁荣。总之，我想聊 SEO 迷思。我知道你有几个东西，而且我们聊过其中几个，我觉得就是人们关于 SEO 相信、但其实错的事。我就问你，人们对 SEO 有哪些常见的错误迷思？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: Probably the biggest one we've said over and over is they even need to do SEO. There's this always default assumption that you've raised money, you have a marketing team, you should do SEO. I think that one is really worth putting to bed is think about that user journey. Should you do SEO? It's a question like, "They ask about other channels, should you do brand..."
turns.zh: 可能我们翻来覆去说的最大一个是，他们甚至需要做 SEO。有个一直默认的假设：你融了钱、你有个营销团队、你就该做 SEO。我觉得那个真值得被放进棺材，就是想想那个用户旅程。你该做 SEO 吗？这是个像“他们问别的渠道，你该做品牌吗……”这样的问题

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: It's a question like they ask about other channels. "Should you do brand marketing? Should you take out an ad in Times Square?" And no one will say, "Well, I just raised a million dollars. I should totally take out an ad in Times Square." And congratulations on being in Times Square, by the way.
turns.zh: 这是个像他们问别的渠道的问题。“你该做品牌营销吗？你该在时代广场买个广告吗？”而没人会说“嗯，我刚融了 100 万刀。我完全该在时代广场买个广告。”而且顺便，恭喜你上了时代广场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: No one will just decide, "Oh, I've got money to burn, let me just burn it." So somehow SEO becomes this thing of like, "Oh, I've raised money. Now, I need an SEO team." So that's I think the first myth that's really important to just put to bed.
turns.zh: 没人会就决定“哦，我有钱烧，让我就烧了”。所以不知怎的 SEO 变成了这种东西——“哦，我融了钱。现在，我需要个 SEO 团队。”所以我觉得那是第一个真重要、该被放进棺材的迷思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. What else?
turns.zh: 太棒了。还有呢？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: Link building. So link building is brand building. So it's thinking about how you're going to build a brand and have people mentioned to you. And when you're doing link building, you're creating a relationship between the piece of content that has linked to you and the product or whatever you're trying to monetize. So that should be link-building. Just getting the idea of getting links on... An HTML link will equal SEO success, again, I think that's completely wrong. And then I mean probably the biggest myth in general is thinking that Google itself is a black box. So I think there's nuances to how you rank, and no one can really unearth what is it that will you be number one and what it is that will make you be number three. But the basic idea of how you build SEO is very simplistic and Google has a best practices guide on what it is that you should be doing, which is build a website that Google can understand, link to the pages in that, write content that is helpful and that users want to read. And those are the basics. And starting with that is how you're going to build an SEO strategy that improves upon it. But the idea of if, "I take all three of these steps right now. I'm guaranteed to be number one," I think is something that is completely incorrect. And there's an assumption that if you do a lot of things around SEO, you're going to be successful. And I think that that's incorrect. (01:28:57): Yes, there are nuances. But for the most part, you get from most... Zero to 10, you can get to step eight by just doing the best practices.
turns.zh: 建外链。所以建外链就是建品牌。所以是在想你怎么建品牌、让人提及你。而当你在做建外链，你是在造那个链向你的内容、和你试图变现的产品之间的一种关系。所以那才是该有的建外链。只是抱着“拿到 HTML 链接就等于 SEO 成功”的想法，再次，我觉得那完全错了。然后我猜总体而言最大的迷思是觉得 Google 本身是个黑箱。所以我觉得你排名怎么排有细微差别，没人能真挖出什么会让你排第一、什么会让你排第三。但你怎么建 SEO 的基本思路非常朴素，而 Google 有个最佳实践指南讲你该做什么——建一个 Google 能懂的网站、链到里面的页面、写有用、用户想读的内容。那些是 basics。从那个起步，就是你建一个在其上改进的 SEO 策略的方式。但“如果我现在把这三步都对，我就保证排第一”这种想法，我觉得完全不对。而且有个假设是如果你围绕 SEO 做很多事，你就会成功。我觉得那不对。对，有细微差别。但大体上，你从大多数……从零到十，你只做最佳实践就能到第八步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow. It sounds very empowering. I like the sound of that. Maybe just on that thread briefly. If someone wanted to start down the road of SEO, I know you're going to be a little bit biased because you help companies with this, but do you recommend bringing someone like you in first or having someone just give it a shot, listening to this podcast, reading some books and blogs, or something else?
turns.zh: 哦，哇。听起来很有赋能感。我喜欢这说法。也许就顺着这条线简短说。如果有人想开始走 SEO 这条路，我知道你会有点 biased 因为你帮公司做这个，但你建议先带个像你这样的人进来，还是让人就自己试，听听这播客、读点书和博客，还是别的？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: Yes, so I am biased. I think they should have the right people give them advice on SEO. So if someone wants to be... If they validated that there is an SEO effort, paying for help on SEO, it goes back to that resource discussion we had before. So if you want to hire a growth advisor, a growth advisor might be very expensive, but you squash a learning curve so you don't make as many mistakes as fast. (01:29:56): If you hire someone in-house, and a lot of times they see this with roles where I'm helping companies hire someone for SEO, they don't have a lot of budget, which means they're going to have someone that doesn't have a lot of experience. So is that the right decision to make? If you're hiring an agency, agencies are typically expensive, and agencies a lot of times get paid on deliverables. So are the deliverables they're doing worth paying for? (01:30:20): An easy deliverable that a lot of agencies produce now is content, but that goes back to our earlier discussion. Do you even need the content? It's very easy for agencies to sell content as deliverable because it's something they actually deliver. Delivering strategy the way most of my growth advising works is very difficult because I don't have a strategy to offer in a proposal because I haven't developed a strategy, and we don't actually see the fruits of that until we implement the strategy. But agencies can end-run that by just saying, "Oh, you pay us on a monthly basis and these are the things we're going to shift to you."
turns.zh: 对，所以我 biased。我觉得他们该让对的人给他们在 SEO 上的建议。所以如果有人想……如果他们验证了确实有 SEO 动作，为 SEO 付费，回到我们之前那个资源讨论。所以如果你要雇个增长顾问，增长顾问可能很贵，但你能压扁学习曲线，这样你不会那么快犯那么多错。如果你雇个内部的人，很多时候他们在那些我帮公司招 SEO 的岗位上看到这个——他们预算不多，意味着他们会找个没多少经验的人。所以那是该做的正确决定吗？如果你雇个代理，代理通常贵，而且代理很多时候按交付物付费。所以他们做的交付物值得付钱吗？很多代理现在产出的一个容易的交付物是内容，但那回到我们早先的讨论。你到底需不需要那内容？代理很容易把内容当交付物卖，因为那是他们真交付的东西。以我大多增长顾问的方式交付策略很难，因为我没个策略能在提案里给，因为我还没开发策略，而且我们真要到实施了策略才看到果实。但代理能绕开那个，就说“哦，你按月付我们，这些是我们会 shift 给你的东西”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that I wanted to touch on, which might be a myth and might not be a myth. But I think you're going to say it's a myth based on what you said about Google being so dominant. There's a lot of talk about TikTok and Instagram replacing Search for people. I actually do search TikTok a lot now for like, "How do I solve this problem? How do I cut a watermelon? How do I, I don't know, find a cup for my baby?" It's really good. What's your take on TikTok and Instagram videos basically replacing a lot of searching for Gen Z, especially, and younger kids?
turns.zh: 我想碰一个，可能是迷思也可能不是。但我觉得基于你说的 Google 这么主导，你会说它是个迷思。有很多关于 TikTok 和 Instagram 在取代人们的搜索的谈论。我现在其实经常搜 TikTok，像“我怎么解决这问题？我怎么切西瓜？我怎么，我不知道，给我宝宝找个杯子？”真的好用。你对 TikTok 和 Instagram 视频基本上在取代很多搜索——尤其对 Gen Z 和更小的孩子——怎么看？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: In the Google Verdict, I think Google's said this before. 63% of Gen Z uses TikTok to search.
turns.zh: 在 Google 判决书里，我想 Google 之前说过这个。63% 的 Gen Z 用 TikTok 搜索。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: Yeah. I think that's just a headline number because it comes down to, you said it over and over in the podcast, user journeys. So there's going to be things that are more appropriate for TikTok or Instagram, and there are going to be things that are more appropriate for Search. So I think if you're doing top-of-funnel discovery, you're going to maybe watch TikTok videos to learn more about the topic. But as you go into the mid-funnel, so say you want to... A popular TikTok search is around travel. So you want to go on a trip. You want to go to Southeast Asia. You don't know where exactly you want to go. So you might want to watch a bunch of videos and see influencers and see experiences. But now you're ready to book. And you want to book a hotel. You want to book your flights. All of that is not going to happen on TikTok. All of that's going to happen on Google Search. So that's the mid-funnel again. (01:32:24): A lot of search will move different places, but ultimately, Google is still the right place to do those searches, to do those mid-funnel searches. So maybe it was more inappropriate that there ever wasn't TikTok for you to get those better experiences. For those top-of-funnel things, you had to suffer through reading awful content that was written only for SEO purposes, and now you get rich dynamic content that comes from TikTok. (01:32:49): And one interesting piece on this is if TikTok does get banned in the US, which looks like it's likely, a company that will pick up all of that users is YouTube. So YouTube has YouTube Shorts. And again, we're looking at a potential monopoly with Google as Google tries to put those YouTube Shorts to solve the problem that TikTok was now solving. So that will be kind of interesting.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得那只是个标题数字，因为它归结于，你在播客里翻来覆去说的，用户旅程。所以会有更适合 TikTok 或 Instagram 的东西，也会有更适合 Search 的东西。所以我觉得如果你在做顶层漏斗的发现，你也许会看 TikTok 视频去多了解这个话题。但当你进到中层漏斗，比如你想……一个流行的 TikTok 搜索是关于旅行。所以你想去旅行。你想去东南亚。你不知道具体想去哪。所以你可能想看一堆视频、看影响者、看体验。但现在你准备好订了。你想订酒店。你想订机票。所有这些不会发生在 TikTok 上。所有这些会发生在 Google Search 上。所以那又是中层漏斗。很多搜索会移到不同地方，但最终，Google 仍是做那些搜索、那些中层漏斗搜索的正确地方。所以也许以前没有 TikTok 给你那些更好体验才是更不合适的。对那些顶层漏斗的东西，你不得不忍受读那些只为了 SEO 目的写的烂内容，现在你拿到来自 TikTok 的丰富动态内容。这点很有趣：如果 TikTok 真在美国被禁——看起来很可能——会接住所有那些用户的是 YouTube。所以 YouTube 有 YouTube Shorts。再次，我们看到一个潜在的垄断，随着 Google 试图用那些 YouTube Shorts 去解决 TikTok 现在在解决的问题。所以那会挺有意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. Google all the way down.
turns.zh: 哦天。Google 通到底。

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A thought I had as you were talking about this idea of mid-funnel versus top funnel is a simple way to think about the mid-funnel is where there's intent. You actually have intent to now buy a thing, a specific thing. Yeah. Cool.
turns.zh: 你聊中层漏斗 vs 顶层漏斗时我有个想法，想中层漏斗的一个简单方式就是有意图（intent）的地方。你真的有意图现在去买个东西、一个具体的东西。对。酷。

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: I mean that's what it is, but it's a buyer journey. So at the top of the funnel, you're curious. You don't know if you have intent. And in the older way of doing SEO where you only focused on top of the funnel, you only focused on rankings as a KPI, which I think is sort of the incorrect way of doing things. There is no intent. So you showed a KPI that matched with a non-user, which matched with a non-buyer. (01:33:55): As you move down the funnel, there is intent. So there is a user and there's less traffic. There's always going to be less traffic at the middle of the funnel. But that doesn't matter because your KPI is closely related to your business metrics.
turns.zh: 我是说那正是它，但它是个买家旅程。所以在漏斗顶层，你好奇。你不知道你有没有意图。而在旧的 SEO 做法里，你只聚焦顶层漏斗，你只把排名当 KPI，我觉得那是种不正确的做事方式。那里没有意图。所以你展示了一个跟非用户、跟非买家匹配的 KPI。当你往下走漏斗，有意图。所以有个用户，而且流量更少。中层漏斗的流量永远会更少。但那不重要，因为你的 KPI 跟你的业务指标紧密相关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do a couple more myths if there's anything else that we missed, and then we'll wrap up and get to our very exciting lightning round. Is there anything else that you think is an important myth that people get wrong about SEO?
turns.zh: 如果还有我们漏掉的迷思，咱们再来几个，然后我们收尾、进入超精彩的闪电轮。还有没有什么你觉得重要、人们对 SEO 搞错的迷思？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: I'll touch on one more myth, which is that technical SEO is an easy solve to any SEO problems. So there's been a lot of Google updates recently. Again, I think... I don't like to defend Google because in reading the Verdict, I think that Google did some pretty evil things. But a lot of what Google has been doing is pushing back on the things that users hate. There's a lot of bad SEO content out there. So Google's trying to get rid of a lot of this bad SEO content in their recent updates. (01:34:46): When sites get hit by these updates, they try to solve the problem that they think happened to them by doing technical SEO. So they'll reach out to me or to someone like me and say, "Can you do an SEO audit and understand why our traffic has suffered?" The reason their traffic has suffered is because they've done things that were not really useful for users and they sort of polluted Google. They need to solve that problem. Technical SEO has a place. So if you have a large website with tens of millions of pages, if you're Zillow, how you link to each listing, if you're Airbnb, how you link and allow Google to crawl a site and understand a site, very, very important. (01:35:23): If you have a hundred-page website that sells a SaaS tool, technical SEO is probably going to be less important. So spending money and time on technical SEO would be a waste of time. So I think that's another big myth is you solve SEO problems with the right SEO solution rather than, "Let's do an audit or let's get better links or my page..." Page speed is another one that... Agencies like to sell on... If things related to page speed, Google keeps changing the words of what that is, but it doesn't matter as much. (01:35:54): Because at the margins, yes, maybe if you're Kayak and you're competing, you get Expedia, and Kayak is maybe slightly faster, maybe that matters. But if you're in a space where you're competing against lots of slow terrible websites, it doesn't matter at all. So spending a lot of money on making that fix is not the right thing to do.
turns.zh: 我再碰一个迷思，就是技术 SEO 是任何 SEO 问题的简单解法。最近 Google 有很多更新。再次，我觉得……我不喜欢为 Google 辩护，因为读判决书时，我觉得 Google 做了些挺邪恶的事。但 Google 做的很多是在推回用户讨厌的东西。外面有很多烂 SEO 内容。所以 Google 在最近的更新里试图干掉很多这种烂 SEO 内容。当网站被这些更新击中，他们试图用技术 SEO 来解决他们认为发生在自己身上的问题。所以他们会找我或像我的人说“你能做个 SEO 审计、搞懂我们流量为什么掉了吗？”他们流量掉的原因是他们做了对用户没真用处、某种程度上污染了 Google 的事。他们需要解决那个问题。技术 SEO 有它的位置。所以如果你有个几千万页面的巨型网站，如果你是 Zillow，你怎么链到每个 listing，如果你是 Airbnb，你怎么链、怎么让 Google 爬一个站点、理解一个站点，非常、非常重要。如果你有个一百页、卖 SaaS 工具的网站，技术 SEO 可能没那么重要。所以在技术 SEO 上花时间和钱会是浪费时间。所以我觉得那是另一个大迷思——你用正确的 SEO 方案解决 SEO 问题，而不是“做个审计、或搞更好的外链、或我的页面……”页面速度也是另一个——代理喜欢拿它卖。如果跟页面速度相关的东西，Google 一直在改那是什么的词，但它没那么重要。因为在边际上，对，也许你是 Kayak、你在竞争，你对上 Expedia，而 Kayak 也许稍微快一点，也许那重要。但如果你在一个跟很多慢、烂网站竞争的空间，那完全不重要。所以在修那个上花很多钱不是该做的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like how you just make SEO feel much more approachable and simple and something that you could just do and not have to again figure out the dark arts that...
turns.zh: 我喜欢你怎么让 SEO 感觉更平易近人、更简单，是你可以就去做、而不必再去搞清那些黑魔法……

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: It is not a dark art. It should be for most things, it is simple. And then there are tons of companies out there get in a lot of trouble, and there's billions of dollars to be made on doing the right SEO. But a lot can be unlocked by very simplistic SEO. PMs that don't really have an SEO background can do enough SEO to make a lot of money for the company without needing to be an SEO expert.
turns.zh: 它不是黑魔法。对大多数事，它该是简单的。然后外面有海量公司陷入大麻烦，而做对 SEO 有几十亿刀可赚。但很多能被非常朴素的 SEO 解锁。没有真 SEO 背景的 PM 能做足够的 SEO，为公司赚很多钱，而不需要是个 SEO 专家。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. That's actually how it worked at Airbnb. The PMs work in SEO were not like historically SEO legends. They were just PMs figuring out SEO and they had a really big impact. So that really resonates with me. Eli, is there anything else that we haven't touched on that you think is important to you or something that you think might be useful to people to leave them with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 我爱那个。其实 Airbnb 就是那样运作的。做 SEO 的 PM 历史上不是 SEO 传奇。他们只是 PM 在搞懂 SEO，而且影响很大。所以那真的跟我共鸣。Eli，在我们进入超精彩的闪电轮之前，还有没有什么我们没碰、你觉得重要、或你觉得对人们有用、想留给他们的？

turns.speaker: Eli Schwartz
turns.en: Yes. So I think we talked about how to decide whether to resource SEO, but we didn't talk about how to understand what the expectations are from SEO. So this is something I came up with while I was working at Faire, which is a very interesting company. So it's F-A-I-R-E. They are a wholesale Shopify. They were launching in a new country, and they wanted to understand what the upside of launching in that country was from an SEO standpoint. So the way most people do SEO forecasting is they do a bottoms-up forecast, which is they look at keywords. So say we want to sell a pair of shoes. (01:37:48): You do a bottoms-up forecast, you go onto a keyword research tool, and they're all fairly the same. Look at how many people search for shoes every month. And then you try to estimate what your ranking would be on that word shoes, and then you estimate what you click through it would be, and then based on that, that's your clicks. And then you get a conversion rate, and that's your bottoms up. (01:38:08): And you make an assumption that the word shoes in that tool didn't capture all the people that search like white shoes and black shoes and running shoes, so you just gross it up. You just pick a number and you gross it by 10, and that's your SEO forecast. (01:38:23): Now, the problem with that is that usually it's too small. So you get this number and now you're pitching to launch in a new country. I want to launch in Japan and sell shoes. And you say, "Well, I think I can get 500 users because based on the way I got here, this is my click-through rate and this is my rankings and I'm 500 users." And no one will ever fund that. That's too small. (01:38:44): Now if you're launching in a new country, it's actually fairly easy to figure out what your SEO upside is because you can take the population in the country. So this is not something Pharoah sells, so I don't have to... So I'm not giving away anything. But say you're launching shoes. You're launching a new product website that you're selling shoes in a country like Japan. (01:39:02): I'm going to guess. I don't know the actual numbers for Japan. So say Japan has a hundred million people and you're selling shoes. And you're not going to sell shoes to a hundred million people. We're only selling shoes to men. And let's just divide it in half. 50% of Japan is men, so we got 50 million people that would buy shoes. (01:39:19): But now, we're also going to say, "Well, there's older people and younger people and we're not selling shoes to them." So now we can take 25 million and cut that in half. And then from there, again, we're selling shoes on the internet. Not everyone buys shoes on the internet. Some people buy shoes in a store. Some people buy shoes on the internet. So you take some percentage rate of the amount of people that are going to buy shoes on the internet and say, "We'll take 10% of our 25 billion people in our market. 2.5 million people buy shoes on the internet and we want to do SEO for 2.5 million people. And our expectation is we want to get this number of market penetration, whether it's 10% or 50% or 100%." And there's your number and multiply that number by the amount of shoes they're going to buy every year and your AOV and there's your forecast. (01:40:07): And that may be inexact. And you can tweak those numbers up or down. You can say, "Well, my AOV was wrong. My market penetration was wrong. I was wrong on the total population. I didn't realize that in Japan, no one bought shoes on the internet." But at any point in time, you can go back and adjust your forecast. Whereas if you're doing this bottoms-up forecast, it's actually in many cases wrong to begin with because the keyword research volume is wrong. (01:40:29): I worked with some really fascinating companies where the largest query in their space was the biggest query. So I worked with WordPress. So WordPress, the word WordPress is the biggest query in the web development space itself. There's no other word that's as big as WordPress. And the number that every single keyword research tool had was completely wrong of what Google Search Console said for the word WordPress is, "When you're building these forecasts based on keyword research tools, that first number that you build the entire forecast off of if it's wrong, your forecast is wrong." So when you do this top-down, it's a TAM forecast essentially. When you do a top-down, you're closer to the truth. Now, you probably aren't going to get to the truth. I've never seen a product plan get to the truth of what it could do, but it will help you make a better decision than if you just guess.
turns.zh: 对。所以我觉得我们聊了怎么决定要不要给 SEO 资源，但我们没聊怎么理解对 SEO 的期望是什么。所以这是我还在 Faire——一家很有意思的公司——时想出来的。是 F-A-I-R-E。他们是批发版 Shopify。他们要在一个新国家上线，想从 SEO 角度理解在那个国家上线的上升空间是什么。所以大多数人做 SEO 预测的方式是自下而上预测，就是他们看关键词。比如我们想卖一双鞋。你做自下而上预测，你去关键词研究工具——它们都差不多——看每个月多少人搜鞋。然后你试图估计你在“鞋”这个词上的排名会是多少，然后估计你的点击通过率是多少，然后基于那个，那是你的点击。然后你拿个转化率，那是你的自下而上。然后你做个假设：那个工具里的“鞋”这个词没抓到所有搜“白鞋”“黑鞋”“跑鞋”的人，所以你就 gross 上去。你挑个数字、乘 10，那是你的 SEO 预测。现在那个的问题通常是它太小了。所以你拿到这个数字，现在你要 pitch 去新国家上线。我想去日本卖鞋。你说“嗯，我觉得我能拿到 500 个用户，因为基于我到这的方式，这是我的点击通过率、这是我的排名、所以 500 个用户”。而没人会 ever 给那个投钱。那太小了。现在如果你在新国家上线，其实相当容易搞清楚你的 SEO 上升空间，因为你能拿那个国家的人口。所以这不是 Pharaoh 卖的，所以我不必……所以我没透露什么。但假设你卖鞋。你在一个像日本这样的国家上线一个新的卖鞋产品网站。我猜。我不知道日本的实际数字。所以假设日本有 1 亿人、你在卖鞋。而你不会把鞋卖给 1 亿人。我们只卖给男人。就除以二。日本 50% 是男人，所以我们有 5000 万人会买鞋。但现在，我们也会说“嗯，有年长的、有年轻的、我们不卖鞋给他们”。所以现在拿 2500 万、再砍一半。然后从那，再次，我们在网上卖鞋。不是所有人都在网上买鞋。有些人在店里买。有些人在网上买。所以你拿会网上买鞋的人口的某个百分比，说“我们拿我们市场里 2500 万人的 10%。250 万人网上买鞋，我们想为这 250 万人做 SEO。而我们的期望是想拿到这个市场渗透率数字，不管是 10%、50% 还是 100%”。那就是你的数字，乘上他们每年会买的鞋的数量、乘上你的 AOV，那就是你的预测。那可能不精确。你可以上下调那些数字。你可以说“嗯，我的 AOV 错了、我的市场渗透率错了、我对总人口错了、我没意识到在日本没人网上买鞋”。但任何时候你都能回去调你的预测。而如果你做这个自下而上预测，它在很多情况下从一开始就是错的，因为关键词研究量错了。我合作过一些真有意思的公司，他们领域里最大的查询就是最大的查询。所以我在 WordPress 工作过。WordPress，“WordPress”这个词在网页开发领域本身就是最大的查询。没有别的词跟 WordPress 一样大。而每个关键词研究工具给的数字，跟 Google Search Console 说“WordPress”这个词的数字完全错。“当你基于关键词研究工具建这些预测，你整个预测建在其上的第一个数字如果错了，你的预测就错了。”所以当你做这个自上而下，它本质上是 TAM 预测。当你做自上而下，你更接近真相。现在，你可能到不了真相。我从没见过一个产品计划到过它能做到的真相，但它会帮你做比瞎猜更好的决定。

turns.zh: 我在飞机上看了个电影《Blackberry》，它看起来像纪录片，所以不知道你看过没，但很迷人。因为它是那种有悬念、而你确切知道它怎么结尾的电影。而且是部那么迷人的电影。我不知道那段历史，但他们曾拥有整个智能手机行业，然后归零。它真的画出了那段旅程，让你想“你永远不能真的躺在桂冠上。你得造人们想要的产品、理解你的用户、持续卖那个产品。”而不是“嗯，我们排第一，这永远不会有事。”很棒的电影。
